31194:
Priscilla, called Prisca by Paul, was with her husband Aquila one of the most important missionary couples of the early church. Expelled from Rome when Claudius ordered Jews out of the city, they settled in Corinth, where Paul lived and worked with them as a fellow tentmaker. They then moved to Ephesus ahead of Paul's long ministry there, and later returned to Rome. In each city a church met in their home.

The couple are mentioned six times, always together, and in four of the six Priscilla is named first, which was unusual in the ancient world and suggests she was the more prominent of the two in the church or of higher social rank. Acts records that both of them took the gifted preacher Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately, one of the few New Testament scenes of a woman teaching a man about doctrine.

Paul says they risked their necks for him and that all the churches of the Gentiles were grateful to them. Their mobility, trade and household leadership make them a window into how the gospel spread through ordinary work and homes.
31195: Priscilla and Aquila are always mentioned together. Priscilla is named first in Acts 18:18, Acts 18:26, Rom 16:3 and 2 Tim 4:19; Aquila first in Acts 18:2 and 1 Cor 16:19. Egalitarians reply that the text does not mark the setting as private versus public in a way that bears on office.

31292:
James was the eldest-named of Jesus's brothers. The Gospels indicate that he did not believe in Jesus during his ministry, but Paul records that the risen Christ appeared to him, and within a few years he had become the leading figure in the Jerusalem church. Paul names him with Peter and John as one of the pillars, and Acts shows him giving the decisive judgment at the council that freed Gentile believers from circumcision.

James represented the Jewish-Christian wing of the church, devoted to the law and respected even by non-Christian Jews for his piety, hence his nickname the Just. He sought to hold together Jewish believers zealous for the law and Paul's Gentile mission, an uneasy task reflected in the tension of Gal 2:12 and Acts 21:20-25. The Letter of James, with its emphasis on practical righteousness and faith shown in works, is traditionally attributed to him.

The Jewish historian Josephus records that he was stoned on the orders of the high priest Ananus in AD 62, one of the few events in the New Testament church independently attested by a non-Christian source.
31293: The Gospels call him one of Jesus's brothers (adelphoi). John 7:5 says the brothers did not believe in him. Paul calls him the Lord's brother, says the risen Christ appeared to him, and names him as a pillar. Acts shows him leading the Jerusalem church and speaking for it. The Letter of James is from James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and Jude introduces himself as the brother of James. The New Testament does not record his death.
31294: Helvidian view (most Protestants and many modern scholars)
31295: James was a son of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus, so a full younger brother (half-brother in terms of Jesus's virginal conception). Adelphos most naturally means brother, and Matt 1:25 and Luke 2:7 (firstborn) are read as consistent with later children. Critics object that adelphos can cover wider kin; supporters reply that the Gospels consistently pair the brothers with Mary.
31297: James was a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage, so an older stepbrother of Jesus, preserving Mary's perpetual virginity. This is attested early in the *Protevangelium of James* (2nd century) and defended by Epiphanius. Supporters note Jesus entrusted Mary to John at the cross (John 19:26-27), which would be odd if she had other sons; critics regard the earlier marriage as unattested in Scripture.
31299: James was a cousin of Jesus, son of another Mary (Mark 15:40) and perhaps identical with James son of Alphaeus. Jerome argued this in *Against Helvidius* (c. 383), noting that Hebrew and Aramaic had no separate word for cousin. Critics observe that the New Testament has a Greek word for cousin (anepsios, Col 4:10) and that Paul distinguishes the Lord's brother from the Twelve; supporters answer that Semitic usage shaped Gospel Greek.
31301: Luther famously called the Letter of James an epistle of straw relative to the chief books (1522 preface), because it seemed to contradict Paul on justification by faith; he later softened his language. Most Protestant interpreters now read James 2 and Romans 3-4 as complementary: Paul attacks works as a basis for acceptance, James attacks a faith that produces no works.

The James ossuary (published 2002), inscribed James son of Joseph brother of Jesus, has been the subject of a forgery trial in Israel (acquittal in 2012 for lack of proof); scholars remain divided on whether the last part of the inscription is ancient.
